study_identification.author_journal_year: Liu et al., Progress in Neuropsychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry, 2024
study_identification.title: Individualized functional connectome abnormalities obtained using two normative model unveil neurophysiological subtypes of obsessive compulsive disorder

study_characteristics.study_objective: To identify potential OCD subtypes based on individualized functional connectome abnormalities obtained using normative models of functional connectivity strength (FCS), and to evaluate differences in clinical variables and functional connectomes between the identified OCD subtypes.

dataset_name.answer: Local dataset from the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: DPABI (Data Processing & Analysis for Brain Imaging); Brainnetome atlas (Fan et al., 2016) with 246 cortical and subcortical regions; slice timing correction; realignment; normalization to standard EPI template; resampling to 3×3×3 mm³; smoothing with 6×6×6 mm³ FWHM Gaussian kernel; detrending; band-pass filtering (0.01-0.1 Hz); regression of Friston 24 motion parameters, white matter signal, and CSF signal; despiking using 3dDespike

quality_checking_detail.answer: Exclusion criteria: translational or rotational displacement exceeding 3.0 mm or 3.0°. None of the subjects were excluded according to this standard. Mean frame-wise displacement (FD) was calculated to assess effects on results.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Single-site study conducted at the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University.

software_tool.answer: Not explicitly stated (likely custom implementation or standard GPR libraries)

response_variable.answer: Functional Connectivity Strength (FCS) for each brain region (246 regions from Brainnetome atlas)

predictor_effects.answer: Fixed effects for age and sex

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study controls for age, sex, and mean FD in statistical analyses, which partially addresses nuisance structure. However, the normative model itself only includes age and sex as predictors, not accounting for other potential nuisance variables like scanner-related factors. The paper mentions FD was used to assess effects but does not clearly state whether it was included in the normative model training. The preprocessing includes regression of motion parameters, white matter, and CSF signals, which addresses some measurement-related nuisance factors.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: For each brain region, a Gaussian process regression model was trained to estimate the normative range of FCS values as a function of age and sex within HCs... We derived distinct patterns of FCS within each subtype and across all patients using a two-sample t-test while controlling for age, sex, and mean FD... Friston 24 motion parameters, white matter signal and cerebrospinal fluid signal were regressed out as nuisance covariates.

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study performed 10-fold cross-validation on the healthy control dataset to evaluate the performance of the Gaussian process regression model. This is a standard approach for validating normative models using non-independent (overlapping) subsets of the same training dataset.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: First, we evaluated the performance of the Gaussian process regression model in predicting FCS values within HCs through 10-fold cross-validation. The standardized mean squared error (MSE) between the true FCS values and predicted values was computed to assess the model's accuracy... The 10-fold cross-validation performed on HCs demonstrated a high level of generalizability in the fitting performance of normative models for FCS, as evidenced by a mean MSE close to 1 (99.94e⁻² ± 5.84e⁻²).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not report validation of the normative model using a completely independent healthy control dataset from the same domain (i.e., a held-out test set that was never used in model training). Only 10-fold cross-validation within the same dataset was performed.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No text in the paper describes validation using an independent healthy control dataset.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not report validation of the normative model using data from a different domain (e.g., different scanner, different site, or publicly available dataset). This is a single-site study and no external validation was mentioned.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No text in the paper describes validation using data from different domains or external datasets.

clinical_dataset.answer: Local dataset from the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University

clinical_groups_age.answer: OCD: mean 23.16; sd 9.34; Subtype 1: mean 24.91; sd 9.59; Subtype 2: mean 18.27; sd 6.21

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (individualized FCS abnormalities); extreme deviations defined as Z-scores exceeding ±1.96 (two-tailed 95% confidence interval)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: K-means clustering algorithm using individualized FCS abnormalities as features, with silhouette values to determine optimal number of subtypes (tested 2-10 subtypes with 100 iterations each); two-sample t-tests (Bonferroni corrected p<0.05) to derive distinct FCS patterns for each subtype versus HCs; demographic and clinical comparisons between subtypes (age, sex, educational level, Y-BOCS total score, illness duration, age of onset, mean FD) using chi-square tests for categorical variables and two-sample t-tests for continuous variables; reproducibility analysis using Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) with 1000 iterations of 90% subsampling and validation with AAL atlas
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Two OCD subtypes with opposite FCS abnormality patterns were identified: subtype 1 (73.74%, n=73) showed decreased FCS in frontal, insular, hippocampal, and pre/postcentral regions, while subtype 2 (26.26%, n=26) showed widespread increased FCS; subtypes differed significantly in age of onset (18.28±10.53 vs 11.49±7.14 years, p=0.003).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling of FCS and k-means clustering, two distinct OCD subtypes were identified with contrasting functional connectome abnormalities. Subtype 1 (73.74%, n=73) exhibited significantly decreased FCS (Bonferroni corrected p<0.05) primarily in the superior medial frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, temporal gyrus, insula, parahippocampal gyrus, hippocampus, precentral/postcentral gyrus, and middle occipital gyrus. Subtype 2 (26.26%, n=26) demonstrated increased FCS across distributed regions including superior medial frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, thalamus, striatum, and middle occipital gyrus. When all OCD patients were pooled, no significant FCS abnormalities relative to HCs were observed, suggesting the differences are obscured at the group level. Demographically, subtype 1 patients were older (t=2.17, p=0.032) and had later age of onset (t=2.52, p=0.014; subtype 1: 18.28±10.53 years vs subtype 2: 11.49±7.14 years). No significant differences were found in educational level (p=0.284), illness duration (p=0.705), symptom severity measured by Y-BOCS (p=0.472), or mean FD (p=0.562). Reproducibility analysis showed high consistency: average ARI of 0.91±0.08 between subsampling results and full cohort; validation with AAL atlas yielded optimal k=2 with ARI=0.43 between atlases. Regarding heterogeneity, 44.44% (n=44) of OCD patients showed extreme negative deviations in at least one region (predominantly in precentral/postcentral gyrus, superior medial frontal gyrus, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, superior temporal gyrus, thalamus, insula, and hippocampus), while 21.21% (n=21) showed extreme positive deviations, though overlap rates in any single region were notably low.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Cross-sectional design limits assessment of subtype stability over time; single-site study requiring independent dataset validation to confirm generalizability; limited clinical information restricting exploration of subtype differences in other clinical aspects; uncontrolled factors including body mass index and alcohol/cigarette use; educational level imbalance between OCD patients and HCs (though no difference between subtypes); lack of external validation of normative model; no investigation of treatment response differences between subtypes
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The identified subtypes reconcile inconsistencies in previous functional connectome studies of OCD. The findings suggest early-onset and late-onset OCD patients have divergent brain connectome abnormalities, providing new insights into neuropathology. The study demonstrates that group-level analyses may obscure important individual-level differences. Future research should investigate treatment response differences between subtypes and validate findings in independent cohorts for personalized diagnosis and treatment strategies.

general_notes.general_notes: This study represents one of the first applications of normative modeling to functional connectivity strength (FCS) in OCD to identify neurophysiological subtypes. The study used the Brainnetome atlas (246 regions) for primary analysis and validated results using the AAL atlas (90 regions excluding cerebellum, and all regions including cerebellum). The normative model demonstrated good performance with mean MSE close to 1 (99.94e⁻² ± 5.84e⁻²) in 10-fold cross-validation. FCS was calculated as the sum of connectivity between a given region and all other regions, with only correlations exceeding r=0.2 included to exclude weak correlations potentially stemming from noise. Whole-brain FCS values were z-score normalized for comparability across participants. The global signal was not regressed during preprocessing because its variance and topography have been found to be altered in mental disorders. All patients were first-episode and untreated (medication-naive). The study was approved by the research ethics committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University and followed Helsinki Declaration principles. Funding was provided by Natural Science Foundation of China and Medical Science and Technology Research Project of Henan province.
